questions.question: What is the difference between a lambda and an anonymous class in Java?
questions.title: Lambda vs Anonymous Class in Java
questions.direct_answer: A lambda supplies the function method of a compatible functional interface and uses the enclosing lexical meaning of `this`. An anonymous class creates an instance of a new unnamed class that implements one interface or extends one eligible class, can declare fields and several methods, and has its own `this`. Java compilers normally translate lambdas through `invokedynamic`, but that translation is not the main language-level distinction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the semantic differences beyond syntax—specifically this reference scoping and the bytecode-level distinction between lambdas and anonymous inner classes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying lambdas are always better or faster, or forgetting that a lambda cannot supply a multi-method contract or introduce its own class scope and `this`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain lexical `this`, local capture, and why compiler translation details should not be confused with the source-level contract.

sections.title: Two Ways to Implement Behavior On-The-Fly
sections.content:
A **lambda** supplies the function method of a target functional interface. An **anonymous class** declares and creates one unnamed class expression that implements one interface or extends one eligible class.

A lambda is ideal when the target contract has one function method and the body is naturally a small piece of behavior. It uses lexical scope: in an instance context, `this` and `super` mean what they mean in the enclosing code. An anonymous class body introduces its own `this`, may declare fields and helper methods, and can implement all methods required by its chosen interface or superclass.

A Java compiler normally emits an `invokedynamic` call site for a lambda, while an anonymous class is commonly compiled as a separate class file. Those are useful implementation details, not promises that make every lambda faster or smaller. Choose from semantics and readability first.

- **Lambda**: functional-interface target, lexical `this`, captured locals must be final or effectively final.
- **Anonymous class**: one interface or one eligible superclass, its own `this`, may contain state and several method bodies.

sections.title: Lambda vs Anonymous Class at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Lambda|~supplies a functional interface method|lexical `this`|captures effectively-final locals|usually translated with invokedynamic
blue|Anonymous class|~one interface or eligible superclass|its own `this`|fields and helper methods allowed|commonly a separate class file
emerald|Choose by semantics|~lambda for a clear function value|anonymous class for class-like state or several methods|measure performance|do not rely on translation shape

sections.title: Anonymous class: verbose boilerplate
Lambda: same behavior, one line
Lambda vs Anonymous Class
sections.content:
| Aspect | Lambda expression | Anonymous class |
|---|---|---|
| Target | Compatible functional interface | One interface or one eligible superclass |
| `this` | Same meaning as enclosing context | Anonymous object itself |
| Body | Supplies one function method | May declare fields, helpers, and several method bodies |
| Local capture | Final or effectively-final locals | Final or effectively-final locals |
| Typical translation | `invokedynamic` call site | Separate anonymous-class file |

sections.title: Choosing Between Lambda and Anonymous Class
sections.content:
Use a **lambda** when implementing a functional interface (one abstract method) and you need clean, readable code—especially for short operations like filtering a stream, defining a Comparator, or handling button clicks. Lambdas shine in data processing pipelines where you're chaining operations: orders.stream().filter(o -> o.getTotal() > 100).map(Order::getCustomerName).

Use an **anonymous class** when you need to implement an interface with multiple methods (like MouseListener with mouseClicked, mousePressed, etc.), when you need instance variables to maintain state across method calls, or when you need the anonymous class's own this reference for callbacks. Also use anonymous classes when extending abstract classes with constructors that require arguments, since lambdas can't call super() constructors.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `this` incorrectly**: in an instance context, `this` inside a lambda means the enclosing object; in an anonymous class it means the anonymous object. A static context has no `this`.
- **Trying to use a lambda for a non-functional interface**: a lambda needs a functional-interface target. Use an anonymous class, a named class, or another suitable implementation for a multi-method contract.
- **Inferring speed from translation**: lambdas commonly use `invokedynamic` and anonymous classes commonly use a separate class file, but neither shape proves a universal performance result.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Functional-interface target**: a lambda supplies the interface's function method
- **Lexical scope**: `this` and `super` retain their enclosing meaning in a lambda
- **Anonymous-class scope**: an anonymous class body has its own `this` and can declare instance state
- **Local capture**: both forms require captured local variables to be final or effectively final
- **Translation detail**: lambdas normally use `invokedynamic`; do not infer a universal performance result from that

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A lambda supplies the function method of a compatible functional interface, while an anonymous class creates an object of a new unnamed class that implements one interface or extends one eligible superclass.

The clearest semantic difference is scope. In an instance method, `this` inside a lambda still means the enclosing object. Inside an anonymous class, `this` means the anonymous object. An anonymous class can also declare fields, helper methods, and all methods required by a multi-method interface; a lambda supplies only one function method. Both forms require captured local variables to be final or effectively final.

Compilers normally translate a lambda with `invokedynamic` and an anonymous class as a separate class file, but that does not prove one is always faster. Use a lambda for concise behavior such as a `Comparator` or `Runnable`. Use an anonymous class when the class-like state, extra methods, or distinct `this` is part of the design.

questions.question: When should you use a Stream instead of a traditional for-loop in Java?
questions.title: Stream vs For-Loop: When to Use Which
questions.direct_answer: Use a stream when a filter, map, grouping, or reduction is clearer as a declarative pipeline. Use a loop when index-aware control, several breaks or continues, checked exceptions, or deliberate mutation makes the flow clearer. Neither is inherently faster. Consider a parallel stream only for a measured, splittable, independent workload with suitable cost and no unsafe shared state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment on abstraction trade-offs—whether you can choose the right tool based on readability, maintainability, and performance requirements rather than defaulting to one approach.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always choosing streams to appear modern, even for simple iterations where a for-loop is clearer and more maintainable—or conversely, avoiding streams entirely due to unfamiliarity.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that changing to a parallel stream changes execution constraints and resource use; it is a measured design decision, not a reason to choose streams in advance.

sections.title: Two Philosophies for Processing Collections
sections.content:
A **Stream** describes a pipeline such as filter, map, then collect. A **for-loop** states each iteration step directly. The better choice is the one that makes the operation and its control flow easiest to verify.

Stream intermediate operations are lazy and compose well for transformations, reductions, and grouping. A loop exposes the index, `break`, `continue`, local mutation, and exception handling directly. Short-circuit stream operations such as `anyMatch` and `findFirst` cover some early-exit cases, but a loop can be clearer when several control paths interact.

A pipeline can be switched to parallel execution, but that does not make parallelism free. Source splitting, encounter order, operation cost, shared common-pool use, side effects, and measurement all matter. A loop can also be parallelised with other concurrency APIs; the choices simply expose different controls.

Neither style is inherently faster. Boxing, allocation, JIT compilation, source shape, data size, and the actual operations determine the result, so benchmark a real hot path rather than relying on a list-size rule.

sections.title: Stream vs for-loop at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Use a Stream|~Declarative pipeline|filter / map / collect chains|reads like the intent|easy parallelStream()
blue|Use a for-loop|~Imperative control|need index or break/continue|mutating external state|simple tight loops
emerald|Watch out|~streams aren't always faster|small lists: loop is fine|no clean early break|trickier stack traces

sections.title: Stream vs for-loop, side by side
Step 1: Consider the Operation Complexity
sections.content: First, evaluate what you're doing with the data. If you're applying a sequence of transformations—filtering, mapping, sorting, or reducing—streams are naturally expressive. Code like list.stream().filter(x -> x > 10).map(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.toList()) is more readable than the equivalent nested for-loops with intermediate lists. Streams eliminate **boilerplate**: you don't declare temporary collections, you don't manage indices. But if your logic requires index access (processing every third element), or if you need to break early with conditions that don't map cleanly to takeWhile or filter, a for-loop is simpler. For simple iteration without transformation—just printing each element or summing numbers—either works, so choose based on team convention and readability.

sections.title: Step 2: Evaluate Performance and Parallelization Needs
sections.content:
Second, measure performance only when the path matters. A stream may add abstraction, boxing, or allocation costs, while the JIT can also optimise both stream and loop code in ways that are hard to predict from source alone. There is no correct universal threshold such as 1,000 elements.

A parallel stream asks the stream implementation to partition the source and execute tasks, normally on the common `ForkJoinPool`. It can help when the source splits efficiently, each element has enough independent CPU work, the reduction is associative, and ordering or coordination costs are modest. It can hurt when work is small, blocking, ordered, stateful, or competing with other common-pool tasks. Benchmark the actual workload and consider whether an explicitly managed executor gives the application better isolation and cancellation control.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a stream when a loop states the job more clearly**: `users.stream().forEach(...)` and an enhanced for-loop are both valid; choose from the surrounding flow rather than novelty.
- **Using parallel streams blindly**: a parallel pipeline normally shares the common pool. Blocking calls, small tasks, ordering, or contention can remove the benefit and make cancellation or isolation harder.
- **Modifying external state in stream operations**: behavioral parameters are expected to be non-interfering and usually stateless. Shared mutation can race in parallel and makes even sequential code harder to reason about.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Declarative vs imperative**: streams describe a pipeline; loops expose iteration and control flow
- **Laziness**: intermediate stream operations wait until a terminal operation starts traversal
- **Parallel execution**: `parallel()` is concise but changes ordering, resource, safety, and performance concerns
- **Non-interference**: stream functions should not modify the source and should normally avoid shared mutable state
- **Measure hot paths**: neither syntax is inherently faster for every workload

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Use a stream when the job reads naturally as a pipeline—for example, filter paid orders, map them to customer IDs, remove duplicates, and collect the result. Use a loop when the index, several early exits, checked-exception handling, or deliberate step-by-step mutation is central to understanding the code.

Both styles can be correct and fast. A stream is not automatically faster, and a loop is not automatically more efficient; the result depends on the source, operations, boxing, data, and JIT optimisation. Parallel streams deserve a separate decision. They normally use the common `ForkJoinPool` and help only when work splits well, is independent and sufficiently costly, and measurements show a benefit. Blocking calls, shared mutation, strict ordering, or common-pool contention can make them a poor fit. Choose the clearest sequential form first, then profile a real bottleneck.

questions.question: How does Optional compare to null checks in Java, and when should you use it?
questions.title: Optional vs Null Checks in Java
questions.direct_answer: Optional is a container that makes a possibly absent return value visible in the method signature. A nullable return relies on documentation or an annotation and is easier to overlook. Optional encourages explicit handling through map, orElse, orElseThrow, and similar methods, but it cannot force safe code because get() still exists. It is mainly a return-type tool; field and parameter use depends on the API and framework constraints.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Optional as an API design tool for explicit contracts, not just syntactic sugar over if-null checks—and that it has appropriate and inappropriate uses.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Optional.get() without checking isPresent() first, which just replaces NullPointerException with NoSuchElementException and defeats the entire purpose of using Optional.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Optional is designed for return types to communicate possibility of absence in the API contract—it's not meant for fields, constructor parameters, or method parameters where null is clearer.

sections.title: Making Absence Explicit in Your API
sections.content:
An **Optional** is a container that is empty or holds one non-null value. It makes a possibly absent return value visible in the method signature. A plain **null** relies on documentation, an annotation, or convention, so it is easier for a caller to overlook.

Optional works well for a lookup such as `Optional<User> findById(id)`. The caller can use `map`, `orElse`, `orElseThrow`, or `ifPresent` to state what an empty result means. It encourages a decision but does not force safe handling because `get()` still exists.

Optional is mainly a return-type tool. Field serialization and JPA mapping support vary, and Optional parameters can add wrapping without clarifying the API. Those uses are design choices, not forbidden syntax.

Calling `get()` without knowing a value exists only replaces a possible NullPointerException with NoSuchElementException.

sections.title: Optional vs null at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|null|~Absence by convention|caller may forget the check|NPE risk at runtime|use clear contracts
blue|Optional<T>|~Absence inside the type|encourages explicit handling|map / orElse chaining|clear return contract
emerald|Rule|~return Optional, not null|prefer it for return values|framework support matters for fields|don't call get() blindly

sections.title: null-based API: NPE waiting to happen
Optional-based API: absence is in the type
Optional vs Null Checks
sections.content:
| Aspect | Optional | Null Checks |
|---|---|---|
| Explicitness | Absence is part of method signature | Requires documentation or code inspection |
| Compile-Time Safety | Forces consumer to handle absence | Easy to forget null check |
| Functional Methods | orElse, map, filter, ifPresent | Requires manual if-else blocks |
| Performance | Small object allocation overhead | No allocation, direct reference |
| Appropriate Usage | Method return types | Fields, parameters, local variables |

sections.title: When to Use Optional vs Null
sections.content:
Use **Optional** as a return type when a method may legitimately have no result, such as `findById`. Return an empty collection instead when ‘no elements’ already has a natural collection value.

For inputs, prefer a required parameter, overload, builder, or domain type when it states the valid choices clearly. A nullable parameter can still be ambiguous, so do not use null merely to avoid Optional.

For fields, model the domain and check the frameworks in use. Optional is not Serializable and is not a portable JPA basic-field mapping, though some serializers add explicit support. Local variables usually need neither Optional nor null if normal control flow can express the state.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Optional.get() blindly**: userOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException when empty. Use an operation that states the empty case.
- **Using Optional fields without checking frameworks**: Optional is not Serializable and is not a portable JPA basic-field type, although some serializers add support.
- **Replacing a clear input contract with null**: Prefer a required value, overload, builder, or domain type; a nullable parameter may be just as unclear as an unnecessary Optional wrapper.
- **Creating Optional.of(null)**: Optional.of requires a non-null value. Use Optional.ofNullable only when adapting a source that may return null.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Container Type**: Optional wraps a value that may or may not be present, making absence explicit in the type system
- **Return Type Design**: Optional is intended for method return types, not fields, parameters, or collections
- **orElse vs orElseGet**: orElse evaluates the default eagerly, orElseGet takes a Supplier and evaluates lazily only if needed
- **map and flatMap**: Enable functional transformations on the wrapped value without explicit presence checks
- **isPresent Anti-Pattern**: Writing if(opt.isPresent()) opt.get() defeats the purpose—use ifPresent, orElse, or map instead

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Optional makes a possibly absent return value visible in the method signature, while null usually relies on documentation or convention. For a lookup, Optional-of-User tells the caller that no user is a normal result. Methods such as map, orElse, orElseThrow, and ifPresent help express that empty path. The type still does not force safe handling, because get on an empty Optional throws. Optional is mainly useful for return values. An Optional parameter often adds wrapping without clarifying the input, and Optional fields need compatible serialization or persistence support. For collections, an empty list is usually the natural no-results value. The practical goal is a clear API contract, not replacing every null with another wrapper.

questions.question: When would you choose an interface with default methods over an abstract class in Java 8?
questions.title: Default Methods vs Abstract Class in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: Choose an interface with default methods when you want to define a contract that multiple unrelated classes can implement (since Java supports multiple interface implementation). Use an abstract class when you need to share state (fields), define constructors, or provide protected methods. Default methods added behavior to interfaces but didn't eliminate the need for abstract classes when you need true inheritance with shared state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that Java's single inheritance limitation still applies and how default methods changed but didn't eliminate the interface-vs-abstract-class trade-off in Java 8.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking default methods made abstract classes obsolete—abstract classes still provide constructors, instance fields, and protected access that interfaces cannot.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the resolution order: a concrete class method wins, then the most-specific interface; an explicit override is needed only for unresolved defaults inherited from unrelated interfaces.

sections.title: Evolution of Java's Abstraction Mechanisms
sections.content:
An **interface with default methods** is a contract that can also provide reusable method bodies. An **abstract class** can provide behavior plus instance fields, constructors, and protected members.

Java 8 added default methods so interfaces such as `Collection` could gain operations such as `stream()` while preserving source compatibility for many existing implementations. Interfaces still have no instance fields or constructors, while a class extends only one class but may implement several interfaces.

Default conflicts follow an order: an inherited concrete class method wins over interface defaults, and a more-specific subinterface wins over its ancestor. Only unrelated inherited defaults that remain equally specific require the class to override. Inside that override it may call an eligible direct superinterface default with `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

sections.title: Interface+default vs Abstract Class
sections.content:
amber|Interface + default|~Behavior, no instance state|multiple inheritance|no constructors|since Java 8
blue|Abstract class|~Behavior plus state|single inheritance|fields + constructors|protected members
emerald|Choose|~need state? abstract class|just shared methods? interface|many parents? interface|template w/ fields? abstract

sections.title: Default method vs abstract class in code
Step 1: Determine if Multiple Implementation is Needed
sections.content: Start by asking: do I expect multiple unrelated classes to implement this contract, or am I modeling a single inheritance hierarchy? If you need multiple implementation—like both Customer and Order implementing Auditable with a getLastModified method—use an interface with default methods. A class can implement many interfaces, so Customer can be both Auditable and Serializable. If you're building a hierarchy where only related classes share behavior—like Shape as a base for Circle, Rectangle, Triangle—an abstract class works because you're modeling true inheritance. The single inheritance limitation isn't a problem here since Circle is-a Shape and nothing else. Default methods work great for **cross-cutting concerns** that span unrelated classes, while abstract classes fit **vertical hierarchies** where subclasses share fundamental characteristics.

sections.title: Step 2: Assess State and Initialization Requirements
sections.content: Second, evaluate whether you need shared state or initialization logic. If your abstraction requires **instance fields**—like an abstract Logger with a protected timestamp field that all subclasses access—you need an abstract class. Interfaces can only have static final constants, not mutable instance state. Similarly, if you need **constructors** to enforce initialization—like an abstract DatabaseConnection that validates connection parameters—use an abstract class. Interfaces don't have constructors because there's no instance to initialize. Default methods in interfaces can reference other interface methods but can't access instance variables. If your behavior is purely algorithmic and stateless—like default void printDetails() that just calls other methods—a default method in an interface works fine. But the moment you need to track state across method calls, you need an abstract class with fields.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming default methods replaced abstract classes**: abstract classes still provide constructors, instance fields, and protected members.
- **Overstating the diamond conflict**: a concrete class method wins over an interface default, and a more-specific subinterface default wins over its ancestor. A class must override only when unrelated inherited defaults remain unresolved; it may then call an eligible direct superinterface default with `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- **Forcing shared state into an interface**: if related subclasses need common instance state and controlled initialization, an abstract class is often the direct model.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Single inheritance**: a class extends one class but may implement multiple interfaces
- **Instance state**: abstract classes can declare instance fields and constructors; interfaces cannot
- **Default methods**: interfaces can share behavior and evolve contracts
- **Resolution rules**: class methods win, then the most-specific interface; unrelated inherited defaults require an explicit override

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Choose an interface with default methods when several unrelated classes share a contract and stateless reusable behavior. Choose an abstract class when related subclasses need common instance state, constructor rules, or protected implementation details. A class can implement several interfaces but extend only one class. Default methods also help evolve interfaces, which is why Java 8 added methods such as `Collection.stream()`. They do not replace abstract classes. If defaults overlap, remember the actual resolution order: a concrete class method wins, then a more-specific interface wins; only unresolved defaults from unrelated interfaces force an override.

questions.question: Can you compare the key Java 8 features and explain how they relate to each other?
questions.title: Java 8 Features Comparison Summary
questions.direct_answer: Java 8 connected several language and library features around functional interfaces. Lambdas and method references are concise ways to supply behavior; Streams use that behavior in pipelines, and Optional uses it for present-or-empty transformations. Default methods helped existing interfaces gain new operations such as `Collection.stream()`. These features support declarative and composable code, but they do not make data immutable or require lambda syntax.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how Java 8 language syntax, functional interfaces, and library APIs fit together rather than listing isolated features.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Streams or Optional require lambdas. Their methods accept functional-interface objects; a lambda or method reference is simply the concise way to provide one.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how functional interfaces connect the features, how default methods aided API evolution, and why none of this guarantees immutability or better performance.

sections.title: How the Java 8 Features Connect
sections.content:
Java 8 added language syntax and library APIs that meet at the **functional-interface** boundary. A functional interface gives behavior a Java type. A lambda or compatible method reference can supply its one function method without the wrapper code of an anonymous class.

**Streams** accept functional interfaces in operations such as `filter`, `map`, and `reduce`. **Optional** accepts them in methods such as `map`, `filter`, and `ifPresent`. Those APIs do not require lambda syntax: an anonymous class could be passed instead, but a lambda is usually easier to read. A **method reference** such as `Order::getTotal` is another concise form when an existing method already matches the target signature.

**Default methods** solve a different problem. They gave interfaces a compatibility mechanism for adding implemented instance methods. That helped `Collection` gain `stream()` without requiring every existing implementation to declare a new body, although source conflicts and behavioral compatibility still need review.

Together, the features make declarative pipelines and callbacks more practical in ordinary object-oriented Java. They do not make objects immutable, prevent side effects, or guarantee faster code.

sections.title: The Core Java 8 Features Together
sections.content:
amber|Functional interfaces|~give behavior a Java type|one function method|target for lambda or method reference|anonymous class also works
blue|Streams|~build processing pipelines|lazy intermediate stages|terminal operation consumes|accept Predicate / Function / Collector
emerald|Optional|~models one value or empty|best known as a return type|map / filter / ifPresent|not a universal null shield
violet|Default methods|~implemented interface methods|aid compatible API evolution|Collection.stream()|conflicts still possible

sections.title: Java 8 Features Working Together
Understanding the Interconnections
sections.content:
**Lambdas are foundational**: Streams, Optional, and CompletableFuture have many methods that accept functional interfaces, and lambdas provide concise implementations of those interfaces.

**Method references simplify lambdas**: `Order::getTotalValue` can be clearer than `order -> order.getTotalValue()` when the lambda only forwards the call.

**Default methods enable evolution**: Collection gained `stream()` and `parallelStream()` without requiring every existing implementation to add a method body.

**Streams use behavior as input**: operations such as filter, map, and reduce accept functional interfaces. Other operations, including count, distinct, and no-argument sorted, do not take a lambda.

**Optional can use lambdas**: map, flatMap, and orElseGet accept functional interfaces, which helps express a possibly absent result as a pipeline.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying Streams depend on lambda syntax**: Stream operations depend on functional-interface contracts. Lambdas, method references, and anonymous classes are different ways to supply them.
- **Assuming functional style guarantees immutability**: stream lambdas can mutate referenced objects or external state. Prefer non-interfering operations, but do not claim the API enforces immutable data.
- **Promising default methods never break code**: they improve source and binary compatibility, but unrelated inherited defaults can conflict and a new implementation can change behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Functional interface**: gives a lambda or method reference its target type
- **Behavior as a value**: a functional-interface instance can be passed, stored, or returned
- **Streams**: use behavior in declarative processing pipelines
- **Optional**: uses behavior to transform or consume a present value while preserving an empty result
- **Default methods**: let interfaces supply inherited behavior, with conflict rules and compatibility caveats

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Java 8's features connect through functional interfaces. A lambda is an expression that supplies the implementation of a functional interface, so APIs can accept behavior without an anonymous-class wrapper. Streams use this in operations such as filter, map, and reduce, while operations such as count and distinct need no lambda. Optional and CompletableFuture also have methods that accept functional interfaces for transformations and callbacks. A method reference is a shorter form when a lambda only calls an existing method. Default methods let interfaces add behavior compatibly; that is how Collection could gain stream() without forcing every existing implementation to add a new method body. Together these features make small declarative pipelines easier to write, while normal object-oriented code remains part of the design.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app using Java 8 streams and lambdas
speakable_v2.hook: Java 8's features aren't a random grab bag. They're one connected system. It's built around one idea, functional code inside an OOP language.

beats.text: Java 8 connected functional interfaces, lambdas, method references, streams, Optional, and default methods. Functional interfaces are the common contract: lambdas and method references supply behavior that APIs can accept.

Before Java 8, passing behavior commonly meant an anonymous class. Lambdas made the same functional-interface contract concise, so stream pipelines and Optional transformations became much easier to read.

items: A lambda supplies the function method of a compatible functional interface.
Streams and Optional accept functional interfaces in operations such as map and filter; anonymous classes would also work.
Method references can replace forwarding lambdas, while default methods help interfaces gain implemented behavior without removing conflict checks.

beats.text: Picture one order pipeline. You call orders.stream. You filter the completed ones, map with a method reference, and collect the result. Here's the non-obvious part. Every step there just runs a lambda behind a one-method interface. That's why these features feel like one toolkit.

items: Saying Streams and Optional require lambda syntax instead of naming the functional-interface contract.
Claiming a stream makes elements immutable or a default method can never create a compatibility problem.

speakable_v2.cap: The shared contract is the functional interface: lambdas and method references provide behavior, Streams and Optional consume it, and default methods helped existing interfaces grow.
